title: What you keep
hook: three Stoic habits that fit your life

segments.voice: Yesterday: where the Stoics stop, the honest edge of the map. Your line was what it leaves open. Did you write your open question down? Day six hundred eighty-seven.

Open almost any kitchen drawer and you'll find the gadgets: a garlic press, an egg slicer, a cherry pitter used once. Then there's what actually gets reached for every night: one good knife, one pan, a wooden spoon. Nobody plans that short list. Use writes it. This year on the path has handed you a lot: morning previews, evening questions, two handles, two cities, the view from above, the ripe olive. Most of it can stay in the drawer. Today: what you keep.
screen: `A DRAWER FULL OF GADGETS.` → `ONE KNIFE, ONE PAN, ONE SPOON.` → `A YEAR OF PRACTICES.`

segments.voice: First, Seneca's advice on books. In one of his earliest letters to Lucilius, he warns against reading too many authors, skipping from one to the next. Food that's thrown up as soon as it's swallowed, he says, doesn't nourish. A plant moved too often never grows. Better to stay with a few great minds and digest them. And each day, choose one thought to carry. That's the spirit of this week: not everything, but a few things, really digested. Second, Epictetus on training. The Stoic word is askēsis: practice, training, the way an athlete trains. Every habit, Epictetus says, is built up and strengthened by the matching actions: walking by walking, running by running. If you want to be good at something, do it. If you don't want a habit, stop feeding it. So the habits you keep are the ones you'll actually do, not the ones you admire. Third, how to choose your three. Ask three questions of each practice from the year. Did I actually use it? Did it change a real day, even once? Does it fit the life I have, with my work, my family, my body, my beliefs? Someone might keep the evening review, the two columns, and delaying an angry reply. Someone else, the morning preview, the view from above, and love for the mortal. There's no right three. Fourth, why three. Few enough to remember without a list. Enough to cover morning, evening and the hard moments in between. Epictetus told his students not to talk about their principles, but to show them by how they live. Three is a number you can show.
screen: `DIGEST A FEW, DON'T SAMPLE MANY.` · `ASKĒSIS: HABITS BUILT BY DOING.` · `USED IT? CHANGED A DAY? FITS MY LIFE?` · `THREE YOU CAN SHOW, NOT TELL.` · then, large: `MY THREE.`

segments.voice: Let the year's practices pass slowly through your mind, like utensils laid out on a counter. The morning preview. The evening questions. The two columns. The other handle. The view from above. Delay. Both cities. Begin now. Notice which ones your hand actually reached for on hard days. Pick up three, one at a time, and keep them out on the counter. Put the others back in the drawer; you're not throwing them away. The bell holds the time.
What you keep: the three Stoic habits from this year that actually fit your life, chosen to be practiced, not admired. Today's word.
Your line: my three. Write your three habits down today, on paper or your phone, somewhere you'll see them next week. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Some people finishing a period of Stoic study choose a small number of practices, often three, that they will keep using daily, and write them down.

pairs: show them, don't talk about them

fork.setup: you've learned dozens of Stoic practices this year. what would Seneca and Epictetus suggest?
options: keep all of them on a long checklist
choose a few and practice them until they're yours
drop them all now the year is over
fork.reveal: Seneca says digest a few; Epictetus says habits are built by doing. A few practiced beats many admired.

original.note: Greek: training or practice, as an athlete trains; the root of ascetic.

trapdoor: what you thought: what you keep from a year of study is a lot of knowledge.
what it means: a few habits, practiced until they're yours, matter more than many ideas admired.
what a scholar hears: Seneca's Letters 2 warns against reading too widely; Epictetus's Discourses 2.18 says every habit is strengthened by corresponding acts; askēsis gives English 'ascetic'.

notes: Letters 2 paraphrased (food that comes up as soon as it's swallowed doesn't nourish; a plant often moved can't grow; stay with a few master thinkers; choose one thought each day). Confirm.
Discourses 2.18 (every habit confirmed by corresponding actions: walking by walking, running by running) and 3.12 (on training, askēsis). Confirm.
Enchiridion 46: don't call yourself a philosopher or talk about principles; act on them. Confirm.
The 'view from above' is referenced as a practice met earlier in the year (e.g. day 647, Scipio's dream). Confirm it was taught.

Audit (year 2, second sample): the moving-house hook and pack-three-in-a-box practice repeated day 518 (What to keep from Seneca) almost exactly, and 'almost a year on the porch' echoed days 686 and 688; hook and practice were rewritten around a kitchen drawer and the few tools actually used. The invented 'one reader keeps...' examples were reworded as hypotheticals.
